Why only forty tokens per second?
2.8 trillion weights, but each token wakes only 104 billion.
At four bits, that's 52 gigabytes per token, minimum.
A weight starts on an NVMe drive.
It's read into host RAM, copied across the PCIe bus, and lands in GPU memory.
The cores only ever compute on bytes that are already in VRAM.
Every hop has its own speed, and the slowest hop sets the pace for everything else.
When you decode one request at a time, every new token forces the GPU to read every active weight once.
For each weight it reads, it does roughly one multiply-add.
That's almost no math per byte — low arithmetic intensity — so the cores spend their time waiting on memory.
The ceiling is simple: bandwidth divided by the bytes you read per token.
Take tiny corp's red kimi box, built to run Kimi K3.
Forty tokens per second means twenty-five milliseconds per token.
From VRAM — four GPUs at 640 gigabytes per second each — you can read 64 gigabytes in that window.
From the NVMe array, at 225 gigabytes per second measured, only 5.6.
So the experts a token needs have to sit mostly in VRAM, and the drives only serve the misses.
Each drive sits on four PCIe 5 lanes: about 15.75 gigabytes per second.
Sixteen of them give about 252 peak, and tiny corp measured 225, eighty-nine percent.
Four drives roughly fill one sixteen-lane link, which is why they're split into four groups, one per IO hub, each next to its GPU.
